podcast.body: Este álbum, lanzado en 1968, consistió en la reinterpretación de obras de Johann Sebastian Bach utilizando un sintetizador Moog. Se convirtió en un hito tanto comercial como artístico, logrando ganar tres premios Grammy y siendo el primer disco de música electrónica en alcanzar el Top 10 del Billboard 200. "Su álbum Switcheton Back, de 1958, desde el pretaobra de Johann Sebastian Bach en sintetizador, fue unito tanto comercial como artístico, ganando tres premios Grammy siendo el primer disco de música electrónica en estar en el Top 10 del Billboard 200."

podcast.body: Released in 1968, this album featured 10 pieces by Johann Sebastian Bach, entirely performed on a giant modular Moog synthesizer unit. The recording process was extensive, taking five months and over a thousand studio hours on a custom-built eight-track recorder due to the synth's monophonic nature and complex sound programming. "The result was an album entitled Switched On Bach, 10 pieces by Johann Sebastian Bach, and everything was played on a giant modular synthesizer unit supplied by Bob Mogue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The album was a massive commercial success and played a crucial role in legitimizing the synthesizer. It demonstrated that synthesizers could be used for sophisticated musical compositions beyond simple sound effects, opening new possibilities for electronic music and garnering critical acclaim. "Not only was it commercially successful, but it drew attention to the capabilities of the synthesizer and the possibilities for electronic music."

podcast.body: This album was recorded by classical musician Walter Carlos using synthesizers, notably without a symphony orchestra, which was considered "heresy" at the time. Carlos collaborated with Dr. Bob Moog to perfect the synthesizer's sounds and control, and the album went on to sell more than a million copies. "And the result was an all-electronic 1968 album switched on Bach, which sold more than a million copies."
